name: Mirtazapine (Remeron)
summary: Sedating antidepressant often chosen when depression comes with insomnia, low appetite, or nausea. Usually taken once nightly. Common trade-offs: grogginess and weight gain.
description: Mirtazapine is an antidepressant that’s famous for two things: sleep and appetite. For a lot of people, it helps them fall asleep faster and stay asleep longer—sometimes from the first night—while mood and anxiety symptoms improve more gradually over a few weeks. The flip side is real: morning “hangover,” weight gain, dry mouth, constipation, and higher cholesterol can show up, especially early on. Like all antidepressants, it carries a suicidality warning in young people and needs close monitoring when starting or changing the dose.
patient_summary: Mirtazapine is an antidepressant that’s often picked when depression is tangled up with insomnia or poor appetite. It’s usually taken at bedtime and can make sleep better quickly, while mood changes take weeks. The common downsides are morning grogginess and weight gain. In younger patients, antidepressants can increase suicidal thoughts early in treatment, so close monitoring matters.

metadata.pharmacologic_category: Noradrenergic and Specific Serotonergic Antidepressant (NaSSA); Tetracyclic

linked_conditions.context: FDA-approved for major depressive disorder in adults. Often chosen when depression includes insomnia, low appetite, or nausea because it can improve sleep and appetite earlier than mood.
Sometimes used as an alternative option when SSRIs aren’t effective or tolerated. Benefits may start within a couple weeks, with continued improvement over 4–6 weeks (and some patients need longer).
Frequently used in psychiatry for sleep when insomnia is tied to mood or anxiety. It’s sedating, especially at lower doses.
Sometimes used when SSRIs cause sexual side effects, either by switching to mirtazapine or using it as part of a strategy to reduce SSRI-related sexual dysfunction.
Occasionally considered as an alternative agent in methamphetamine use disorder when first-line options aren’t effective or tolerated.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to mirtazapine or any component of the formulation (including severe skin reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, DRESS)
Use with monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) concurrently or within 14 days of stopping an MAOI
Starting an MAOI within 14 days of stopping mirtazapine

efficacy_response.patient_text: With mirtazapine, sleep and appetite can improve early (sometimes within days), while mood and anxiety benefits usually build over 1–2 weeks and keep improving over 4–6 weeks. If you’re taking it for panic symptoms, the timeline can be slower—don’t judge it after only a few nights.

pharmacokinetics.onset: Sleep/sedation can be rapid; antidepressant effects often begin in 1–2 weeks with continued improvement over 4–6 weeks
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensive hepatic metabolism (CYP3A4 major; CYP1A2, CYP2D6, CYP2C9 minor) via demethylation and hydroxylation
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Can be taken with or without food

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Mirtazapine is an antidepressant that’s often picked when depression isn’t just “sadness,” but also insomnia, low appetite, weight loss, nausea, or high agitation. It’s taken once daily (usually at bedtime). It is not approved for pediatric patients.
items: {link:condition:major-depressive-disorder:Major Depressive Disorder (MDD)}: Depression symptoms with or without anxiety, especially when sleep and appetite are falling apart
Depression with insomnia: Helpful when the depression picture includes trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking too early
Depression with low appetite or weight loss: Can be useful when food is a battle and energy is low
off_label: Panic disorder (alternative option when SSRIs don’t work or aren’t tolerated)
Insomnia tied to depression or anxiety (common psychiatry use, not FDA-labeled)
SSRI-associated sexual dysfunction (switching strategy in some cases)
Methamphetamine use disorder (alternative agent in select cases)

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Everyone’s different, but mirtazapine has a pretty recognizable “signature.” Here’s what people commonly describe:

quotes: I took it and my brain finally shut up.
I didn’t just fall asleep—I stayed asleep.
It felt like a heavy blanket for my nervous system.
items.note: Sedation is often stronger at lower doses (like 7.5–15 mg) and can feel less intense at higher doses for some people.

quotes: I slept great… and then woke up like I got hit by a truck.
The first week I felt foggy until late morning.
I could not do early meetings on this.
items.note: This often improves over days to a couple weeks as your body adapts, but not always.

quotes: I was hungry like… aggressively hungry.
My cravings were wild at night.
It helped me eat again, but I gained weight fast.
items.note: Appetite increase can be a feature or a bug depending on your baseline.

quotes: Sleep improved first. Mood followed a couple weeks later.
I woke up with cotton mouth every day.
I had to up water and fiber or I paid for it.

items.category: Activation or mood switch (rare, but important)
quotes: I got weirdly wired and irritable.
Sleep got worse and I felt sped up.
It tipped me into a mixed-feeling spiral.
items.note: If you have bipolar risk (personal or family history), any antidepressant can trigger hypomania/mania—this needs clinician-level attention.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Mirtazapine often helps sleep and appetite early, while mood benefits build more slowly.
key_points: First 1–3 nights: Sedation and sleep support can show up quickly (especially at lower doses)
1–2 weeks: Early mood/anxiety improvement may start to appear
4–6 weeks: Typical window for fuller antidepressant response (sometimes longer, especially for anxiety/panic symptoms)
~2 hours: Time to peak blood level after a dose
20–40 hours: Average half-life (supports once-daily dosing, usually at bedtime)

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Mirtazapine is a solid antidepressant option, especially when depression comes with insomnia, poor appetite, nausea, or a lot of internal agitation. Many people notice sleep and appetite changes early, which can make the “waiting period” for antidepressant mood benefits feel more tolerable. For panic symptoms, improvement may start within a couple weeks and continue building over 4–6 weeks (and some people need a longer trial).
sections.clinical_details: In practice, mirtazapine is often selected for its calming nighttime profile and lower tendency to cause SSRI-type sexual side effects. The trade-off is metabolic and sedation burden: weight gain, increased appetite, and morning grogginess can limit long-term use for some patients. Dose changes should be evaluated over weeks, not days, unless side effects are severe.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Young people starting antidepressants need close monitoring for suicidal thoughts, worsening mood, or unusual behavior changes—especially in the first 1–2 months or after dose changes.
sections.black_box: Antidepressants increased the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in pediatric and young adult patients in short-term studies. Closely monitor all antidepressant-treated patients for clinical worsening and for emergence of suicidal thoughts and behaviors. Mirtazapine is not approved for use in pediatric patients.
other: Do not combine with MAOIs (or within 14 days of stopping/starting): dangerous interaction risk
Sedation is common early on and can impair driving and reaction time—treat it like a sleep medication until you know your response
Weight gain and lipid increases are common enough to matter clinically—plan for monitoring, not vibes
Hyponatremia/SIADH can happen (older adults are higher risk): confusion, weakness, unsteadiness, headache can be warning signs
Rare but serious blood count issues (neutropenia/agranulocytosis): fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers, or infections need urgent evaluation
Rare but serious skin reactions (SJS/TEN/DRESS): any new widespread rash, blistering, facial swelling, or fever + rash needs immediate medical attention
Activation of mania/hypomania can occur (especially without a mood stabilizer in bipolar-spectrum patients)
Serotonin syndrome is rare but possible, especially when combined with other serotonergic meds
Orthostatic dizziness can happen: stand up slowly, especially early in treatment or if you’re prone to low blood pressure
QT prolongation and dangerous rhythm issues have been reported postmarketing: higher concern if you have heart risk factors or take other QT-prolonging meds
patient_counseling: If you’re 18–24 (or caring for someone who is), treat the first 1–2 months like a monitoring period: mood shifts, agitation, impulsivity, or suicidal thoughts need immediate attention.
Take it at bedtime unless your prescriber tells you otherwise. Don’t “test” it right before you need to drive.
Expect appetite changes. If weight gain is a dealbreaker, talk early—don’t wait until it’s a mess.
Call your clinician urgently for fever/sore throat + feeling unusually sick (blood count concern), or for severe rash/blistering (skin reaction concern).
Tell your clinician if you have any history of bipolar disorder, mania/hypomania, or a strong family history—this changes the risk math.
Avoid mixing with alcohol or other sedatives unless your prescriber explicitly okays it.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common: drowsiness, dry mouth, increased appetite, constipation, weight gain, and cholesterol/triglyceride changes. Lower doses can feel more sedating than higher doses for some people.

common.incidence: Very common (reported around half of patients in short-term studies)
common.patient_note: This can be the whole point (better sleep) or the reason people quit (morning hangover). If you feel unsafe to drive in the morning, that’s real—adjust timing, dose, or plan with your prescriber.
Hydration helps, but it can still be annoying. Sugar-free gum or lozenges can make a difference.
This can feel like cravings that hit hard, especially at night. If weight is a concern, plan meals/snacks intentionally rather than winging it.

common.incidence: Common; significant weight gain can occur with short- and long-term use
common.patient_note: Some people gain quickly. If this starts early and bothers you, bring it up early—there are options.
Water + fiber + movement matter. If you’re prone to constipation, be proactive from day one.

common.incidence: Common (cholesterol increases are reported more often than triglycerides)
common.patient_note: This is why labs matter. You don’t have to guess—check and track.

serious: Suicidal thinking/behavior changes in younger patients, especially early in treatment or after dose changes: urgent evaluation needed
Severe allergic/skin reactions (SJS/TEN/DRESS): blistering rash, mucous membrane sores, facial swelling, fever + rash: emergency care
Severe neutropenia/agranulocytosis: fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers, infections: urgent evaluation
Mania/hypomania or mixed activation: decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, irritability, impulsivity: contact clinician urgently
Serotonin syndrome (rare, higher risk with other serotonergic meds): agitation, confusion, sweating, tremor, muscle rigidity, fever: emergency care
Severe hypertriglyceridemia and pancreatitis (rare): severe abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting: urgent evaluation
Movement disorders (rare): akathisia, dystonia, dyskinesia, restless legs: report promptly
QT prolongation/torsades (rare): fainting, palpitations, dizziness: urgent evaluation
Priapism (rare): painful prolonged erection: emergency care

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Mirtazapine can interact dangerously with certain antidepressants, antibiotics, and other serotonergic or sedating medications. Always tell your prescriber what you’re taking—even “supplements.”

items.with: MAOIs (phenelzine, tranylcypromine, isocarboxazid) and IV methylene blue
items.risk: Contraindicated. High risk of severe reactions including serotonin toxicity.
items.action: Do not use together. Wait 14 days between stopping an MAOI and starting mirtazapine, and 14 days between stopping mirtazapine and starting an MAOI.

items.risk: Serotonin toxicity risk has been reported with serotonergic combinations; newer evidence suggests the absolute risk may be low, but it’s not zero.
items.action: If linezolid is medically necessary, use with close monitoring for serotonin syndrome symptoms (agitation, confusion, tremor, fever, sweating, muscle rigidity).

items.with: Other serotonergic medications (SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs, triptans, tramadol, lithium, some migraine meds, St. John’s wort, MDMA)
items.risk: Increased risk of serotonin syndrome, especially with multiple serotonergic agents or dose increases.
items.action: Use cautious combinations and monitor. Seek urgent care for severe agitation, confusion, fever, rigidity, or rapidly worsening symptoms.

items.with: Alcohol, benzodiazepines, sedating antihistamines, sleep meds, muscle relaxants
items.risk: Additive sedation, impaired coordination, falls, blackouts, poor judgment.
items.action: Avoid or minimize. If combined, do it only with a clear plan from your prescriber and treat driving/operating machinery as off-limits.

items.with: Other QT-prolonging medications (selected antipsychotics, some antibiotics, some antiarrhythmics)
items.risk: Higher risk of rhythm problems in susceptible patients.
items.action: Use caution if you have heart disease, electrolyte problems, or multiple QT-prolonging meds. Consider ECG monitoring when risk is elevated.

items.with: Medications that lower sodium (some diuretics) or increase SIADH risk
items.risk: Greater chance of hyponatremia/SIADH, especially in older adults.
items.action: Monitor sodium, especially after starting or increasing dose.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Stopping mirtazapine suddenly can cause withdrawal-type symptoms for some people. If you’ve been on it for more than a few weeks, tapering is usually the move—both to reduce withdrawal and to catch returning symptoms early.
key_points: If treatment lasted ≥4 weeks: taper gradually over about 2–4 weeks as a common starting approach; go slower if you’ve had withdrawal before or you’re on higher doses or long-term treatment.
If treatment lasted 2–3 weeks: tapering over 1–2 weeks is often reasonable.
<2 weeks of treatment: many people don’t need a formal taper, but individual sensitivity varies.
If withdrawal symptoms are intense: return to the prior dose and taper more slowly.

Withdrawal symptoms reported: dizziness, nausea/vomiting, tingling sensations, insomnia, anxiety/panic, irritability, restlessness, vivid dreams/nightmares, and (rarely) mood elevation or hypomania after stopping.
Typical onset window: symptoms can begin within 1–7 days after stopping (even after a taper in some sensitive patients).

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Mirtazapine is usually dosed once daily, most often at bedtime because it can be sedating—especially at lower doses. Dose changes are typically made no more often than weekly so you can tell what’s side effect vs. what’s benefit.

adult.depression_initial: 15 mg PO once daily at bedtime
adult.depression_titration: Increase by 15 mg increments at intervals of at least 1 week based on response and tolerability
adult.depression_max: 45 mg/day (some trials have evaluated up to 60 mg/day, but higher dosing increases side-effect burden and should be specialist-guided)
adult.anxiety_sensitive_start: 7.5 mg PO once daily at bedtime may be used by some clinicians as a gentler start in patients who are sensitive to early antidepressant side effects (jitteriness, nausea, dizziness)
adult.panic_initial: 15 mg PO once daily at bedtime (alternative option when SSRIs are not effective or not tolerated)
adult.panic_titration: Increase by 15 mg at intervals of no less than 1 week based on response and tolerability
adult.panic_typical: Around 30 mg/day in many clinical uses (individualized)
adult.panic_max: 45 mg/day as a usual ceiling in practice; higher doses up to 60 mg/day have been evaluated but require careful risk–benefit monitoring
adult.sleep_offlabel: 7.5–15 mg PO at bedtime is commonly used when insomnia is a major target symptom (off-label; balance benefit vs. next-day grogginess and weight gain risk)

sections.simple_explanation: Most people take mirtazapine once nightly. Sleep and appetite effects can show up early, but mood and anxiety benefits usually take weeks. Lower doses can feel more sedating than higher doses for some people.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Mirtazapine can be used in special situations, but dosing and monitoring change when pregnancy, older age, kidney disease, or liver disease enters the picture. Decisions should be shared and individualized.
sections.pregnancy: Mirtazapine crosses the placenta. Available data have not shown a clear increased risk of major birth defects, but the data are limited. Untreated depression and anxiety during pregnancy also carry real risks, so decisions should balance maternal stability and fetal/newborn safety. If medication is used, aim for the lowest effective dose of a single agent and monitor symptoms regularly with a validated tool. Encourage enrollment in the National Pregnancy Registry for Antidepressants when applicable.
sections.lactation: Mirtazapine and its metabolite appear in breast milk. Reported relative infant doses in available case data are generally below common safety thresholds, and some reports describe no observed sedation or feeding problems—still, infants should be monitored for excessive sleepiness, poor feeding, and poor weight gain. If starting an antidepressant for the first time postpartum in a treatment-naive breastfeeding patient, some guidelines prefer other agents; if mirtazapine has been effective and the risk–benefit favors continuation, it may be reasonable with monitoring.
sections.pediatrics: Not approved for pediatric use. Antidepressants increase suicidal thoughts and behaviors in pediatric and young adult patients in short-term studies; close monitoring is required when antidepressants are used in younger populations.
sections.geriatrics: Use with caution. Older adults may have reduced clearance and are more vulnerable to sedation, falls, and hyponatremia/SIADH. Consider a lower starting dose (such as 7.5 mg at bedtime) and monitor sodium closely when starting or adjusting the dose, especially in patients ≥65 or those on diuretics or with prior low sodium.
sections.hepatic: Clearance is decreased and half-life is increased in mild to moderate cirrhosis, increasing risk of dose-limiting sedation. In preexisting cirrhosis (Child-Pugh A or B), consider starting at about 50% of the usual indication-specific starting dose and titrate cautiously with close monitoring; some expert guidance suggests a practical maximum around 30 mg/day in cirrhosis. In Child-Pugh C, consider alternative agents; if used, start low (about 50% of usual start) and titrate cautiously with close monitoring.
sections.renal: Use with caution because clearance decreases with kidney impairment. For eGFR ≥30 mL/min/1.73 m2, no routine adjustment is commonly required. For eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2 or for dialysis/CRRT settings, consider starting 7.5–15 mg once daily and titrate slowly with close monitoring for sedation and other adverse effects.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Suicidality and clinical worsening: monitor closely during the first 1–2 months and during any dose changes, especially in patients 18–24
Mood switching: screen for bipolar risk before starting; monitor for hypomania/mania or mixed features after starting or increasing dose
Sedation and safety: daytime sleepiness, driving impairment, falls (higher risk in older adults and when combined with other sedatives)
Weight and appetite: baseline weight/BMI and regular follow-up; track rapid early gain and nighttime eating patterns
Lipids and metabolic markers: lipid profile (cholesterol/triglycerides) at baseline and periodically, especially if weight increases
Sodium (hyponatremia/SIADH risk): check sodium when initiating or increasing dose in older adults or high-risk patients
CBC when clinically indicated: educate patients to report fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers, or infections (rare neutropenia/agranulocytosis concern)
Renal and hepatic function: baseline and periodic monitoring in patients with known impairment or higher clinical risk
Serotonin syndrome monitoring when combined with serotonergic meds: agitation, confusion, tremor, sweating, rigidity, fever
Orthostatic symptoms: dizziness or near-fainting, especially early in treatment or in patients on blood pressure meds
QT risk assessment when clinically relevant: consider ECG monitoring in patients with cardiac history, electrolyte issues, or multiple QT-prolonging medications

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Mirtazapine is taken by mouth once daily. There are standard tablets and orally disintegrating tablets (ODT) for people who prefer them or have trouble swallowing pills.
items: Tablets (generic and Remeron): 7.5 mg, 15 mg, 30 mg, 45 mg
Orally disintegrating tablets (generic and Remeron SolTab): 15 mg, 30 mg, 45 mg
Administration (ODT): Keep in blister until use. Peel back foil, remove with dry hands, place on tongue, let it dissolve—no water needed. Do not chew, crush, or split.
Excipient considerations: Some tablets may contain lactose. Some ODT products may contain phenylalanine (aspartame)—important for patients with phenylketonuria (PKU).

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Mirtazapine works differently than SSRIs. It blocks presynaptic alpha-2 receptors, which increases release of norepinephrine and serotonin. It also blocks certain serotonin receptors (5-HT2 and 5-HT3), and strongly blocks histamine H1 receptors. That H1 blockade is a major reason it’s so sedating and why it can drive appetite and weight gain.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Mirtazapine is often a “strategic pick” rather than a default first choice. It shines when depression is tied to insomnia, low appetite/weight loss, nausea, or when SSRI-type sexual side effects are a big problem. It’s not a great match when weight gain, metabolic risk, or daytime sedation would significantly worsen a patient’s quality of life. For anxiety and panic, it’s typically an alternative option when first-line approaches (like SSRIs/SNRIs and therapy) aren’t effective or tolerated. As always: diagnose bipolar disorder correctly before prescribing antidepressant monotherapy.

seo.title: Mirtazapine (Remeron): Uses, Dosage, Side Effects, Sleep Benefits & Weight Gain
seo.description: Mirtazapine (Remeron) for depression and anxiety symptoms: bedtime dosing (7.5–45 mg), how fast it helps sleep vs. mood, common side effects (grogginess, weight gain), serious warnings, interactions, and tapering guidance.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.a: Mirtazapine is FDA-approved for major depressive disorder (MDD) in adults. In psychiatry, it’s commonly chosen when depression comes with insomnia, low appetite, weight loss, or nausea. It’s also used off-label in some cases for panic symptoms or when SSRI sexual side effects are a major issue.

faqs.q: Is mirtazapine basically a sleep medication?
faqs.a: It’s an antidepressant, not a sleeping pill—but it can be very sedating, especially at lower doses. That’s why it’s usually taken at bedtime. For some people, the sleep benefit is the first noticeable change, even before mood improves.

faqs.q: How long does mirtazapine take to work for depression?
faqs.a: Sleep and appetite changes can show up early. Mood benefits usually start to appear around 1–2 weeks and continue improving over 4–6 weeks. If you’re taking it for panic or anxiety symptoms, the timeline can be slower and sometimes needs a longer trial.

faqs.q: Why do people say lower doses are more sedating?
faqs.a: Mirtazapine strongly blocks histamine (H1), which causes sedation. At lower doses, that histamine effect can dominate. At higher doses, increased norepinephrine signaling can partially offset sedation for some people. It’s not universal, but it’s common enough that clinicians plan around it.

It can, and it’s one of the most common reasons people stop it. It can increase appetite and cravings—often at night—and significant weight gain can happen in both short- and long-term use. If weight gain is a major concern for you, talk about it early so you can make a plan (or consider alternatives).

faqs.q: Does mirtazapine have fewer sexual side effects than SSRIs?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Many people experience fewer SSRI-style sexual side effects on mirtazapine, which is why it sometimes comes up when SSRIs cause sexual dysfunction. That said, everyone’s biology is different, and the trade-off may be appetite/weight or sedation.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol on mirtazapine?
faqs.a: It’s a bad idea. Alcohol can stack with mirtazapine’s sedation and make you more impaired, more dizzy, and more at risk for falls or poor judgment. If you drink at all, do it cautiously and only after you understand how the medication affects you—and ideally with your prescriber’s guidance.

faqs.q: What medications should not be mixed with mirtazapine?
faqs.a: MAOIs are the big one: do not combine them, and keep a 14-day gap when switching. Also use caution with other serotonergic medications (due to serotonin syndrome risk) and with other sedating meds (due to additive impairment). If you take multiple QT-prolonging medications or have heart risk factors, ask whether ECG monitoring makes sense.

faqs.q: Do I need to taper off mirtazapine?
faqs.a: If you’ve been on it for more than a few weeks, tapering is usually recommended. A common approach is tapering over 2–4 weeks after ≥4 weeks of treatment, slower if you’ve had withdrawal before or you’re on higher doses or long-term treatment. If withdrawal symptoms are intense, you may need to return to the prior dose and taper more slowly.

Reported symptoms include dizziness, nausea/vomiting, tingling sensations, insomnia, anxiety or panic, restlessness, irritability, vivid dreams/nightmares, and (rarely) mood elevation. Symptoms can start within 1–7 days after stopping.

faqs.q: Is mirtazapine safe in pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: Pregnancy and breastfeeding decisions are individualized. Available data have not shown a clear major birth defect signal, but the data are limited, and untreated depression/anxiety also carries risks. In breastfeeding, mirtazapine appears in milk and infants should be monitored for sedation or poor feeding. If you’re pregnant, planning pregnancy, or breastfeeding, discuss a shared plan with your prescriber and consider enrolling in the National Pregnancy Registry for Antidepressants.

faqs.q: What should I do if I miss a dose?
faqs.a: If you remember the same night, you can usually take it—unless it’s close to morning. If it’s already late or you’ll need to drive early, it may be safer to skip and take your next dose at the regular bedtime. Don’t double up the next night unless your prescriber specifically tells you to.
